utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you begin, Mr. Karadzic, Judge Baird has a couple of questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, as I studied your evidence over the weekend, I realized that there were certain areas where -- small areas where I might need some assistance. Now, it's possible I might have passed them along the way, but all the same, I would need your assistance in these very small areas. My first question has to do with the opening of the corridor for the passage of the column. Now, Pandurevic and Muminovic arrived at this truce and Pandurevic opened the corridor, and in his report he said he let out 5.000 individuals. He -- if I might paraphrase here, he conceded for a certain number of soldiers getting out, but those who passed through were unarmed. So I apprehended that he was saying fundamentally the bulk of that 5.000 was civilians. Now, Borovcanin -- Borovcanin's forces were part of the forces that Pandurevic was using to fight the column, so he was, as it were, in medias res, he was in the middle of things, and between 6.00 and 8.00 on July 16, Pandurevic submits his interim report. At 1300 hours on the 16th, Borovcanin submitted his report. And in his report, Dr. Butler, he stated that Pandurevic opened a 1-kilometre-wide corridor to allow the Muslim soldiers to get out. He said the bulk of the enemy column, and his understanding was about 2.005, soldiers managed to break through to Nezuk. So Borovcanin had a different view of the composition of the column. What I'm wondering, Mr. Butler, is how did his superiors react to this -- their superiors react to the striking difference in the two reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, what I believe if you look at the sequence of events that follows is that Colonel Pandurevic, by his own admission in the interim combat report, made a decision to let the column through and that he sought to downplay the fact that he had allowed soldiers to escape by seeking to characterise or to downplay the amount of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, the first thing that comes to mind is Colonel Pandurevic and his people weren't close enough to know whether or not those soldiers got out unarmed or not. The second point is, as noted by the commission that came up on the 17th to investigate matters, one of the roles of that commission on the 17th of July was to determine whether or not Colonel Pandurevic's actions were so out of line as to potentially relieve him of command of the Zvornik Brigade or make that recommendation to General Mladic. The army was not happy with that decision to let these soldiers go, the motivation, of course, being that by letting them go, they will face them again in the future. So that is a fundamental difference in how the column is described by Colonel Pandurevic who has a particular reason to want to characterize the column as either unarmed or more civilian in nature, because he is responsible ultimately for letting it go, versus Colonel Borovcanin who did not make that decision and consequently there are no ramifications against him for whether or not the column managed to fight its way out or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But were there ramifications against Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. And I believe that if you look at the 18 July 1995 interim combat report, that is Colonel Pandurevic's long explanation in part as to why he let the column go, the fact that his brigade had taken a significant number of casualties not only during the operations against the column but even previously to that and that this was Colonel Pandurevic explaining to his superiors what his justifications were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes. My question is did they accept it? Was it accepted at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Pandurevic was not relieved of command of the Zvornik Brigade, so his explanation was accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see. I see. Thank you. Now, my second question touches to a certain extent also on the column. You said that the column was allowed to pass between the 16th and the 17th, and the lines were then re-closed with hundreds, if not more, trapped behind those closed lines, and now reports from the Zvornik Brigade that prisoners were being taken from the 18th to the 21st. Now, you said those prisoners have not been accounted for, and you deduced that somewhere in close proximity to where those prisoners were capture, they were summarily executed by either the soldiers or the police who captured them. Now, are you saying then, Mr. Butler, that there would have been several execution sites?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that there were a number of small-scale execution sights. One example that I cite is that on both the 16th and 17th of July, 1995, that is vehicle log from one truck from the 7th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade where the driver of that vehicle actually noted down numbers of prisoners that were being transported by that truck on that day. You see no accounting of those particular prisoners anywhere at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. If one assumes that these people were handled in what would have been the appropriate manner, even in accordance with the VRS's regulations, that truck would have travelled to the Zvornik Brigade or another designated area. Those prisoners would have been dropped off there under the guard to the higher headquarters, which would be the Zvornik Brigade, and they would be accounted for and ultimately moved toward Batkovici. In effect, the same thing that you start seeing happening on the 22nd of July, 1995, but you see no evidence of that. The truck goes to a remote location and then returns back to the battalion headquarters. So I believe that there are a number of examples from the period of the 17th of July till the 21st of July where there are various combat reports that -- or other documents that reflect the Zvornik Brigade or the police forces in the Zvornik Brigade area encountering Muslim groups, and there's no accounting for any prisoners being taken by any of them until the July 22nd report by the Zvornik Infantry Brigade where for the first time they produce a number that says, "We have captured this many prisoners," and perhaps more importantly, actually asked the Drina Corps command for instructions as to how to handle them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But there was never any tangible evidence to support this deduction, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, the only actual noted execution would be what I believe is referred to as the Nezuk execution, which occurred by -- which was occurred by a group of soldiers from the 16th Krajina Brigade who were operating under the command of the Zvornik Brigade at the time. So I believe that is again one vignette story that talks about the fact that a group of soldiers were apprehended and were summarily executed shortly after their captured by the unit that captured them. My belief is that that story played out on a number of occasions until the 22nd of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I thank you very much indeed. Dr. Karadzic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic's interim report on the 18th of July referred to by Mr. Butler admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is P00181.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at the interim combat report that was just mentioned, P181.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the mean time while we are waiting, Mr. Nicholls, how about the -- the report about the execution by 16th 1st Krajina Corps members? Have you admitted that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'll look, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Otherwise you'll deal with it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- during your re-examination [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, please. Do we agree, Mr. Butler that, on the 18th of July, this report stated that allegedly another brigade of theirs had still not pulled out? Given the fact that the sentence following this one states, as was confirmed in other documents, that they had divided themselves up into brigades at the very beginning of the breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is, I think, referring to the last -- the middle lines of paragraph 1 where it is noting -- this is again Colonel Pandurevic's explanation of what he believes that the enemy situation is and how the brigade -- or how the 28th Division sought to withdraw out of the former Srebrenica safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here he mentions their brazen behaviour and unexpected moves they made. Were you able to observe that there were instances of fake surrenders during which a surrendering Muslim soldier would detonate a bomb, thus killing himself and the Serb soldiers approaching?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, my analysis is based off of the documents. I don't know whether that did or did not occur or if testimony has been heard relative to that. I am aware that there are some reports with respect to the - excuse me - the situation and that event occurring in the Bratunac area on the 12th and the 13th from the column there, but I don't believe that I've ever heard reports of that occurring from the column in the Zvornik Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you wonder what such unexpected moves meant and this brazen conduct as described in the report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it when one looks at the various reports from Colonel Pandurevic in context, it's his belief that despite the fact that militarily his forces were in place and should have had -- been able to defeat parts of the column or at least stop various parts of the column's attack, because of the casualties that were occurring, that the column or the leadership of the column was so desperate to escape from behind the territory of the VRS that they were making attacks that caused significant casualties, and they were just not being deterred by those casualties. So it was, as Colonel Pandurevic himself notes, a very desperate battle by -- against enemy forces that were extremely determined to break out. So that is what I take by his various reports with respect to the brazen and unexpected moves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also took note of the fact that in General Pandurevic's words, who -- he was still colonel or lieutenant-colonel at the time, that he suggests that there were more losses than -- than were captured enemy personnel.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure where he may make that suggestion, but I can certainly concur with the fact that in light of the casualties and the combat that was going there, I take it that the enemy losses in both killed and wounded far exceeded any number of prisoners that were at least documented by the Zvornik Brigade as being captured on the 16th and the 17th and the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it is the second paragraph of item 1. The enemy suffered significant casualties and dozens were captured. This would reflect, more or less, what you have just said; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the documents you studied, did you come across a piece of information that General Karisik of the police spoke with me? I don't know. It is mentioned in the documents, and I will probably be able to show it during my Defence case. In any case, he asked me to protect Colonel Pandurevic for having made that move. First of all, did you come across the piece of information that General Karisik informed me about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For your first question, no, sir, I am not aware that General Karisik did or did not inform you. I have not seen a document to that -- to that -- that would reflect that, so I do not know that that would have occurred. As part of your second question, in light of the information that I am aware of, that particularly General Mladic was very unhappy with Colonel Pandurevic's decision, it would not surprise me to know that individuals who were supporting Colonel Pandurevic would have approached you directly on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, no objection. Mr. Karadzic may be thinking of D02002. That's an intercept which refers to Karisik talking to the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While you are on your feet, Mr. Nicholls, with respect to the question by Mr. Karadzic to Mr. Butler whether there were instances of fake surrenders during which a surrendering Muslim soldier would detonate a bomb, have we seen such document, and which also would tell him not to take prisoners or something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not that I'm aware of. There's one incident in the Sandici area where -- where there were reports of a Muslim who was surrendering throwing a hand grenade. I think there was actually testimony about that from a protected witness not very long ago, but there's no report I'm aware of, written report, saying don't take any prisoners because of this danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I will leave it at that. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just one moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic even went up the ranks and in 1996 made it general, made it to become a general?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Colonel Pandurevic, like most officers in the VRS, at the conclusion of the war received a one-grade promotion to the rank of colonel, and in -- I believe it was December or late November of 1996, when then President Plavsic essentially reorganised the Main Staff to become a General Staff and relieved General Mladic and most of the Main Staff officers of their positions, then Colonel Pandurevic was appointed to be the assistant commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs. Essentially he took General Gvero's job and was subsequently promoted to the rank of general-major.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: Did you come across an instruction about arresting and detaining POWs, an instruction which was supposed to be issued on the 15 of April, 1995, by the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of a number instructions through the various course of the conflict that were published by various military levels as to the proper handling of prisoners of war once they would be captured. Again, I may very well have seen that 15 April 1995 document. If you wish to show it to me I can comment on it, but I don't remember the details of it off the top of my head, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look, then, at 65 ter 2063. As you probably know from other cases, as well as from theory and practice, what measures can be taken in terms of POWs; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a general question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess -- I mean, there -- there's two things. I mean, a general sense certainly -- and as reflected by this particular document, there were -- or there was an established process in place for dealing with prisoners for two particular reasons. One, they wanted to, of course, safeguard the prisoners, and they wanted to obtain information of intelligence value. The second thing that they are aware of is that there's what we would call an operational security issue, recognition that down the line that a prisoner may be exchanged in the future and as a result that prisoner should not be taken places or shown things that might be of a sensitive military nature, so that in the event that that individual is exchanged, that prisoner doesn't himself become a source of information about what he learned about the VRS after his capture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that POWs are not to be shown to the media? They are not supposed to be exposed to any humiliation before the public or in the media as part of their status of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm aware of those as general provisions of the Geneva Conventions and associated protocols, and I believe they're also codified as such in the SFRY regulations on the application of those conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you to look at the document. Have you taken note of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least the page that I'm -- I can look at. If you're going to ask me any additional questions, I would like to see the second page as well, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask all the participants to go through the document briefly so that I don't need to read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we go to the third page of the document, please, sir, at least in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just feel free to -- to ask them to leaf through the document once you have read it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next page, please, in English. Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now go back to page 1. Is it true that from the security administration of the Main Staff they had received a warning that there were violations, because it says here -- it outlines in detail the procedure during the detention or arrest of persons violating rules and regulations. [As read] "We submit to you the instruction inform -- inform military police unit with instruction and act upon the provisions listed." This is what Popovic is passing on from the Main Staff. Now, these provisions, are they consistent with what you know about the internationally laid out procedures that govern the treatment of POWs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense that even though they talk about the arrest and detention of POWs and other persons, in that context I take it they're talking about RS and, you know, Republika Srpska citizens who might be arrested for some crime related to the military as well. Yeah, these -- these instructions as such, there's nothing in these instructions that I see that would suggest that they violate the SFRY applications on the rules of the law of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, would you agree with me that the first sentence of the "instruction" speaks about POWs and is issuing a warning that violations have been noticed in the treatment of POWs; that is to say, the soldiers of the enemy army? And also under item 1, it reads under 1: "All prisoners, members of the enemy army are to be handcuffed on their hands, tied with anything available immediately after their capture. They are to be searched and all items are to be seized apart from their clothing and footwear." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is what instruction 1 says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, is it reasonable to assume that if you find personal papers on somebody such as ID, passport, watches, ammunition, et cetera, would it be reasonable to assume that this person had not been captured beforehand? And I'm talking about the belongings found on dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, again, these particular instructions apply to what should have happened in the context of individuals being captured and treated in an appropriate manner. Now, whether or not the failure to comply with those types of instructions or to make, as you've noted, the fact that an individual may have -- still have papers on him or may still have a watch and everything else and is subsequently found in a grave somewhere, I don't know that that would be proof that that person could not have been a prisoner at some point prior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can one deduce, then, that those on whom -- whose bodies nothing was found had been captured previously?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I don't -- I don't deduce one way or another whether or not the presence of a watch or a document or family items would or would not prove that. If I actually had to take a criteria of equipment to use, what I would suggest is that the presence or the absence of military weapons and equipment in a particular grave site would be a more determinative factor. For example, while -- because soldiers may be rushed or lazy or sloppy, they may not confiscate identity cards, they may not track these people, they may miss personal items, I would suggest that under no circumstances would soldiers searching prisoners that they've just captured allow the prisoner to remain with weapons or ammunition or other items of immediate military value.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Did you ever see that an enemy soldier, whether he was killed in combat or in killing, have you ever seen such soldiers being buried together with his arms and weapons, or were those weapons confiscated as trophies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, my experience is that clearly individuals who are battle-field casualties are not buried with their weapons. They may be buried with other military equipment that was either damaged or is otherwise too covered in biological materials as to be effectively cleaned. So in that particular sense, the -- you know, you wouldn't normally see those individuals buried with weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can Mr. Butler please be shown item 3 on the next page -- or, rather, on the next page, because my copy is rather bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is a description of how to transport the prisoners, how to prevent them from escape, and the possibility of observing that you yourself noticed? It includes the possibility to have them blindfolded, their hands tied, and even their feet could be tied?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. Securing a prisoner in that manner to prevent potential escape, as well as to prevent the prisoner from observing things would be an acceptable practice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2243, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you base your findings exclusively on the documents that were accessible to you, or did you yourself check the veracity of these documents, or did you acquire some documents on your own?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer the last question first, any documents that I may have acquired, I did so under the umbrella of the Office of the Prosecutor as a result of my participation in searches, interviews, things of that nature. As to the second question, as to the veracity of the documents, one, setting aside the fact that in almost all of the cases, particularly of the documents that we used in the early portions of the trials in the Krstic and the Popovic -- I'm sorry, the Krstic and the Blagojevic cases, those documents came out of searches and seizures that the Office of the Prosecutor made from inside the military facilities of the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade. So we were, of course, able to assume at face value that the documents that we'd seized were at least in fact authentic. We found multiple copies of other documents as they passed them forth back to headquarters. So we were able to, you know, continue to authenticate and verify many of the documents. And finally, in my particular opinion, the documents that we have reflect the situation that's occurring on the ground during those particular days. It corresponds very closely to those incidents and issues. So, you know, that is the third component of it. And finally, during the course of interviewing various officers of the VRS, many of these documents were shown to these officers who acknowledged that they were either part of creating or producing these documents, and they also sought to explain what these documents meant in a military context to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your experience elsewhere in the world and your expertise with regard to the military, did you notice that in this particular instance the fact that we had people's army and we had local soldiers who had already suffered casualties and lost family members on both sides, so my question is did you notice any other formal -- of behaviour other than strictly military behaviour?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in armed conflict soldiers who are raised locally are going to have personal issues and experiences with conflicts. I suggest to you that that is known not only within the VRS but in all professional military forces. This is why the officer corps of those armies receives the training that it does and why it has the responsibilities that they do to enforce discipline and to enforce the rule of law among the soldiers that they're responsible for commanding. What happened with respect to the personal experiences of individual soldiers within the Republika Srpska and in Bosnia and Herzegovina in losing family members in a conflict is not radically different from what happens in other areas of armed conflicts globally. The fact is that professional militaries recognise that. Professional militaries study history as well as anyone else does, and that in almost all armies - and I say in this particular context certainly within the JNA and the regulations that were adopted by them by the VRS - that fact was recognised and that they had the appropriate regulatory, disciplinary, and even legal means to enforce discipline among their soldiers to prevent or at least mitigate the impact of those issues. I would note that that was made clear by the Main Staff as early as 1992 when guidance was published to the corps reflecting the various criminal and military disciplinary issues that commanders could anticipate facing through the course of the conflict. Not only did they deal with certain issues with respect to desertion, failure to serve, but there's also a particular component in there with respect to the obligations of commanders in preventing or investigating war crimes. So these are not unanticipated events by any military, and they certainly were not unanticipated by the officer corps of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe I wasn't quite clear when I put my question. Do you believe that the VRS was a professional army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS as a total, as most militaries are, are made up of soldiers, most of who are conscripts. They're not professional. However, I believe that the officer corps of the VRS not only was professional in the sense that many of the officers of the VRS were also serving officers of the federal army. Even those VRS officers who were reserve officers had some amount of training prior to the conflict from their -- the rank that they held within the JNA. So I do believe in that particular context the officer corps was professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice how many troops did the VRS have and how many professional officers they had?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a troop number off hand, but certainly the percentage of soldiers to officers, I mean probably you have a situation where 10 per cent of the force, maybe 15, were officers, and the remainder were soldiers. And frankly, more importantly, one of the issues that the VRS systemically had that was problematic was that there was a lack of junior officers at the company -- or at the platoon and the company level, and as noted by the records, many of those junior-level officers were not really officers at all. They were conscripts who had shown the necessary ability and the willingness to take those lower levels of command and were given those lower levels of command because of a result of it. They were often not properly trained in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I tell you that the Army of Republika Srpska for the most part always had --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question, and slow down when you are saying the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that the Army of Republika Srpska mainly had between 210.000 and 225.000 troops, out of which number professional officers accounted for hardly 2.000, and as you rightly noticed, most of them had higher ranks, would you agree that this is way beyond the requirements?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Way below the requirements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, sir, it -- whether -- whether it was or was not, I would note several factors. First of all, if it falls within the 10 per cent range, which I gave earlier, and secondly, I would argue that even though the number of professional officers was low, at least within the context of what the JNA might have in their -- in their view as to what the ratio would be, the fact is that the necessary structures, the necessary laws, the necessary regulations existed to be able to adequately enforce discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But what I'm saying is it's not a question of numbers. It is a question of the ability and the willingness of the senior officials to enforce discipline within the structures that exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not asking you anything about from the point of view of enforcement. I am just asking about whether you comprehended what was the essence of the VRS. If I -- my math is correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you didn't simply ask the numbers. You asked whether Mr. Butler agreed -- would agree that that is well beyond the requirements. So you asked about his opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, but this is not 10 per cent. In his response, he said that this number of officers is consistent with his view that 10 per cent is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is 1 per cent; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. Clearly I haven't had enough coffee this morning to do math.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever notice that the majority of soldiers of the VRS lived and stayed in their own homes rather than in barracks and that rotations took place and that they would spend a number of days on the front line and then a number of days back home?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe for the majority of the VRS that was the practice that was undertaken. Even though military commanders did not -- senior military commanders did not approve of it, the lower-level military commanders in light of the circumstances continued that practice throughout most of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you noticed that in view of the territorial principle of both the VRS and the Army of B and H, that many soldiers knew each other from pre-war peacetime and that they shared some history and some past experiences?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't talk about the big global picture with respect to Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I think that if one looks at strictly the Srebrenica-related crime bases and some of the testimony that has come out and some -- it's even reflected in some of the documents that have come out of particularly the actions related to prisoners or captors knowing exactly who the prisoners are, from what villages they are, and what they did pre-war, there was a great deal of commonality between the military forces in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You noticed quite accurately that there were far fewer killings in Potocari and that there were many more police officers in army than in Bratunac. Did it ever happen that individuals would go to detention places seeking specific people from specific villages with a view to either liberating them or taking them elsewhere? So here we have a completely personal approach. Have you ever noticed this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, it is one of the phenomenons that is noted by a number of witnesses who testified that through the course of their detention in and around the Bratunac area, that individuals from local areas -- or individuals from the local area would be calling out at these various temporary detention places or on vehicles and trucks looking for individuals whom came from certain villages or certain other locations again that, you know, was familiar to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 5, item 15, of your amalgamated statement, you speak about the collection of additional resources of the MUP of Republika Srpska, because they were tasked with completing the transportation of the remaining civilians from Potocari. Did you know that one additional unit, the so-called Jahorina Detachment, was deployed in Potocari, forming a circle defence in order to protect the Muslim civilians from unauthorised and irresponsible attacks. For the benefit of other participants, I can say that this was corroborated by Witness KDZ084.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I am aware that on the 12th of July, it was not only Sekovici police, it was the 1st PJP and 1 Company from the Jahorina training area that were in Potocari. I'm not familiar with the witness testimony in that particular case, so I can't comment one way or another as to what the company's individual actions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to observe that during the night between the 12th and the 13th of July in Potocari there were no VRS personnel whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, sir. I know that there was a police presence there. I know that there was a military presence there during the day. I have no information which would confirm or deny that the VRS completely left the compound at Potocari during the evening hours of 12 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I just ask the basis for putting that assertion, the factual basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I took that to be a question, but I can ask Mr. Karadzic whether it is your submission that there was no military between the 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, we heard about that here from some witnesses that the military wasn't present. I can't give you an exact reference at this point in time. I simply wanted to see with this witness if he was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why don't you ask him whether he knew that whether there was any presence of military without necessarily causing some confusion. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your paragraph 5.24, Tisca-Luke, you say that the refugees were forced to get off the vehicles and continue to the Muslim-held territory on foot. Do you believe that a bus full of refugees could approach the confrontation line, and who would then be held responsible if such a bus were to be hit by a Zolja, a hand-held rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First off, in that particular context where the individuals were taken and coming off the buses, the road was blocked for the most part for vehicle traffic going back and through, so I assume that they left the buses there and had to walk those final several kilometres because the road had on both sides had been made so it was impassable to vehicle traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So they were not forced. It was the only way for them to cross over to the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see in certain UNPROFOR reports that the first several groups were awaited with distrust and dissatisfaction as the Muslim army didn't know what the whole thing was about, and that there were even tensions between those arriving and those who awaited them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with your second assertion that certainly the Muslim forces on the ground there would not have been immediately aware, particularly from the first wave of buses that came in, what was going on. Those individuals were, if I recall, accompanied by a Dutch United Nations officer who was able to lay out the framework of what was happening and why these people were showing up at this particular location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take a certain position in terms of the cause of death of those found in mass graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that throughout the investigative process with respect to the mass graves identified in the Zvornik area that forensically those courses of death have been termed. As I noted in my report and the analysis and testimony, my role in that part was not to analyse the fact that -- how they died, but was to be able to look at all the other military operations that were occurring in context and be able to provide information back to the investigative teams as to whether or not the locations of the primary grave sites corresponded to locations of known combat activity, and it was my opinion - and remains my opinion - that of the four main primary sites in the Zvornik Brigade area, which would be Orahovac, the Petkovci dam, the Drina River site at Rocevic, and Branjevo Farm, that none of those locations saw significant combat activities or any combat activity for that matter, to be clear, on the day that those individuals were killed at those sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you follow testimonies in this case in order to update your knowledge, and did you follow the recent testimony by Drazen Erdemovic and Amor Masic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the testimony of Mr. Erdemovic from previous trials. I have followed no testimony for -- related to this specific case here. My current workload just does not allow me the time and ability to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you allow for the possibility that some graves were filled up in stages? For example, the grave at Branjevo Farm had previous burials and the burials came in stages. Erdemovic confirmed it as having been informed of it at the time on the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Erdemovic did not confirm that the grave was filled up in stages. Another complete misstatement of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please be precise when you cite the evidence given by a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that Erdemovic confirmed it -- [In English] Erdemovic confirmed it as having been informed of it at the time on the 16th of July. [Interpretation] I didn't say that Erdemovic could see that. Apparently a guard had told him that there had been burials previously. We can find that in Erdemovic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Be precise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that other sources, as well as Witness Masovic, confirmed that more graves contained the bodies of those who had been killed as early as 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, what I can say is I do not know what individual witnesses have testified. I am aware that as part of the overall forensics process that, particularly now, there has been for the last five or at least eight years, maybe even longer, a robust process by which to DNA and identify the remains in the graves and, of course, cross-index the identities of those individuals in the graves with when they were identified as missing off of the various ICRC and other lists. So I expect that there is a scientific way that has been undertaken to be able to distinguish individuals who were killed in July of 1995 versus individuals who were killed -- or at least -- or at least identified as missing in earlier stages of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that the DNA methods cannot ascertain either the time of death or time of burial or cause of death?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, you're now kind of migrating out of an area which I have anything other than a layperson's experience with. What I can say is I am aware that there are other investigative and forensic techniques that the investigation teams through the years have used to ascertain those issues, but again, I have no particular expertise in those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 7.72. Do you recall what alternative measures to accommodating prisoners were proposed by Colonel Pandurevic? It is page 80 in of the Serbian of your amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, referring to that, and this brings us back to the 15 July 1995 interim report, my interpretation is that he's talking about the prisoners in this context, and I don't believe he's offering an alternative to accommodating them other than potentially letting them go. There's nothing in this document which suggests that he's suggesting that they move to another location or anything else. It simply says, "If no one takes responsibility, I will be forced to let them go." I am, of course, aware that Colonel Pandurevic himself offers a different interpretation to this, and I just thought I needed to mention that under -- under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'll read out the second quotation by Pandurevic from item 7.72, and I would kindly ask the interpreters to interpret it in the spirit of the Serbian language, especially in the terms of the phrase "I would be forced let them go." It says following: "This command can no longer take care of these problems, as it has neither the material or other resources. In case no one took over this responsibility, I would be forced to release them" or "to let them go." [In English] I suppose this -- this is "to release them," better, more accurate than "to let them go." [Interpretation] Obviously, the genus of the language would require the term "to release them" instead of "to let them go through."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not see a semantic difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic is saying, "If I can no longer take care of them, I will set them free."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, frankly, how I interpret this particular comment. Again given the time of what is occurring and where the prisoners are, even at this particular time that he's aware of this and he's writing this, there are still prisoners still alive at Rocevic who have not been killed, as well as prisoners that are alive at Branjevo and at the Dom of Kulture. So when I evaluate this with other information and documents relating to this, I take this that Colonel Pandurevic is aware of the prisoners. He is aware that they are being executed. He is aware of the significant drain that the obligations to guard these prisoners, kill these prisoners, and then bury them is having on his military unit. And it's a time when he has no military reserves left. The threat of the column continues to grow each hour. It is a reflection on his part that he has actions that he can take relating to the prisoners that would not make his superiors at the Drina Corps and the Main Staff happy. So he is seeking to use that issue as leverage to get additional resources to deal with the situation in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, no objection, but that's -- just to make it easy for the record, that's P00138 is exhibit number of the report we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, with all due respect, aren't you speculating a bit too much given the fact that we have a crystal clear text? There are no forces at his disposal to take care of the prisoners, and unless another command took care of them, his only alternative for him was to set them free. How do you come to your conclusion that he was aware of the killings? Let's stick with the text. How does this text imply he was aware of the killings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, again taking this document in context with all of the other things that are occurring and what Colonel Pandurevic knew and should have known, first of all, Colonel Pandurevic does not return to his area until the morning of the 15th of July. So I do take it that he's not going to have an immediate awareness of what has been happening in the Zvornik Brigade area other than what he has received in reports and various telephone calls. I understand that shortly after his return to the Zvornik Brigade area, and in fact his headquarters, there is a meeting that he sets up with all of the relevant military and police commanders who are now engaged in the Zvornik area, and that all aspects of what has been happening on the ground are going to be briefed to him by all of these individuals. So they're going to tell him what the situation is with the enemy forces. They're going to tell him what the situation is with all of the friendly forces, the police and military forces. I understand that the issue of prisoners being stored in the area also came up. So Colonel Pandurevic, just by virtue of being a competent and diligent military commander, is going to have all of this information. Now, the next piece of information that I relate to is the last sentence or, I guess, the only sentence of the paragraph above that, the obligations of security and restoration of the terrain, the phrase is "asanacija," which is a medical term relating to the burying of bodies and biological wastes. Who's -- if they're not killing the prisoners, just who is Colonel Pandurevic concerned about burying? So he must know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That would be my next question. The remark in the brackets "SIC," is something you inserted or does it figure in the original text next to "asanacija terena"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I say we should bring up the report and -- then, Your Honour, the one we're talking about. We might as well look at the report rather than quotes from the report -- in Mr. Butler's report. I'm speaking of the interim combat report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, while we're waiting for that document, do you remember who put that "sic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure. Like I said, I have to look at the document. I know that from previous cases that it's not a clean translation between the phrase or the word in Serbo-Croatian "asanacija" and the English translation "restoration of the terrain." I put it in my English language one to highlight that fact that one should go back to the Serbo-Croatian explanation of "asanacija." You know, in English "restoration of the terrain," you know, could reflect, you know, moving a hole on a golf course somewhere. It doesn't accurately reflect the type of activity which was done which is most accurately reflected in the definition of "asanacija" in various JNA military lexicons or dictionaries. So that is why I put the phrase "sic" in English, to prompt somebody to go back and look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the legal provision in our body of law concerning "asanacija terena" following floods, combat, et cetera, and what does it entail? Could you provide us with a brief answer if possible, as I have a small number of other documents I wish to cover.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's not a legal term. It's -- basically it's a technical term at least in a military context. It reflects to burying the bodies of individuals who are killed, and of course it could apply to a nonmilitary context, but essentially it is the disposal of biological waste projects that are a result of combat, flood, or other disasters in a proper manner to preclude diseases from breaking out as a result of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. How much more time would you need to conclude your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do my best to conclude in 15 to 20 minutes, and I believe Mr. Nicholls will need some time as well. I will do my best to conclude in 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll continue in the next session. Before we break, I would like -- I'm minded to give a couple of rulings. On the 11th of April, 2012, the accused filed a motion to admit transcript excerpts pursuant to Rule 92 ter, Branko Djeric, in which he requested that the Chamber admit pursuant to Rule 92 ter transcript excerpts of the previous testimony of forthcoming Prosecution witness -- actually next witness, Branko Djeric, which are favourable to his case and which have been omitted from the amalgamated statement proposed for admission by the Prosecution. The Prosecution filed its response on the 19th of April, 2012 in which it states that, as requested by the accused, it contacted the witness in order to confirm whether these excerpts accurately reflect his testimony, and the witness indicated a preference for answering any additional questions and review any additional materials in court. The Prosecution therefore submits that the motion is moot and that in any event, the excerpts may not be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter at this stage. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution seeks to tender a 30-page amalgamated statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter. In order for this statement to be admitted, the Prosecution shall go through the Rule 92 ter formalities, including asking the witness to confirm whether the amalgamated statement accurately reflects what he would say if asked the same questions again. If the accused wishes to ask the witness about those parts of his previous testimony that have not been included in the amalgamated statement and which he considers to be favourable to him, then he may do so by posing these questions directly to the witness during his cross-examination. The motion is therefore denied. Because of the witness's position and his proximity to the accused, as well as the number of areas on which the accused wishes to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber expects the accused to conclude, complete, his cross-examination in four hours' time. On a separate note, on the 17th of April, 2012, the Prosecution filed the Prosecution motion pursuant to Rule 92 quinquies to admit a transcript of prior testimony of Mr. Milan Tupajic and associated exhibits. The Chamber would be assisted by hearing from the accused as soon as possible and therefore orders pursuant to Rule 127 that the accused file his response, if any, no later than Wednesday, 25 of April, 2012. That should be possible, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, you know, we usually file these responses ahead of the dead-lines. This is a particularly problematic motion, and we -- I actually tried to -- I worked on it this weekend, and I think it's going to make me the rest of this week, because this is the first -- at least there's been no public decision on this Rule before, and I think our response is going to be very comprehensive, and we believe that -- I think it's just going to take us longer. So if you could give us until the 1st of May, which is the next day after the weekend, I think we would actually need that in this case because it's an issue of first impression and has a number of elements which we dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's fair enough, Mr. Robinson. Then I expect you to file it by 1st of May, Monday next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's actually Tuesday, because Monday is a holiday, but we will file it on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And lastly, Mr. Tieger, we'll hear from you very soon about the submission from the Defence on the commencement of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break now for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. May we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to the issue raised by Mr. Robinson, are parties in discussion as to the confidentiality, provisional confidentiality, of the exhibit admitted during the testimony of specific witness, for example, 122?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's proceeding in two ways, Mr. President. We're proceeding apace on the formal response. Mr. Robinson and I have also had brief discussions about it to see if there was some avenue, some middle ground, that might obviate the need for a specific decision by the Chamber. We, unfortunately, haven't come to any meeting of the minds on that as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So isn't this correct: We don't have the note that we have in your document as far as sanitisation of the terrain is concerned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand what you mean, "We don't have the note that we have in your --" I don't -- I'm not tracking the question. I think it's probably a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, probably. I -- I meant sic, I meant that note. It is not in the original. Let's see how it's been translated in the document itself, "asanacija," sanitisation. Restoration, is that it, restoration of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I understand it, the phrase "asanacija" is translated into English as restoration of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you put "sic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, to highlight the fact that I don't believe that the English language translation, even though I understand it's the literal translation, accurately reflects what the true definition is. And again, that's why I always default back to "I believe" in my narrative. There is a footnote there where I actually use the definition that we pulled out of one of the Yugoslav National Army lexicons to explain exactly what the term is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What you saw in the law, in our law, that has to do with "asanacija," did that have to do with burying executed persons or assination [as interpreted] -- or "asanacija" in the sense of restoring the area after fighting or after a natural disaster?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you couple the phrase and with Colonel Pandurevic's report on the 15th and the engineer vehicle log which talks about the involvement of the engineer equipment, the locations that it's occurring, and the fact that it's nowhere near the battle-field in the various times, the conclusion - and I believe the only logical conclusion that can be drawn - is that that particular phrase and the "asanacija" that occurred in the mass graves are individuals who are a result of the executions that occurred in the Zvornik Brigade area from the 14th through the 17th of -- or the 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, does he mention that the enemy has sustained major losses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, if we take that report as well, that report of Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, how do we decide that "asanacija" is execution rather than being the burial of these multitudes of people who had lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I would remind you that first of all, the significant battles which were occurring on -- or they were winding up on the 15th of July, 1995, that he's discussing, the first of the two mass graves is already installed both at Orahovac and Petkovci. So just by virtue of chronology alone the graves at Orahovac and at Petkovci cannot apply. I would also that for the graves in other locations, Rocevic and Branjevo, which were installed, started -- or basically, you know, were dug up -- or dug into initially, so I guess it's installation on the 16th and 17th of July, for those bodies to be populated in -- for those graves to be populated with bodies, what would have had to have happened is that during the actual course of conflict, an area that was littered with mines and ordnance and combat operations, that Colonel Pandurevic's troops were essentially going into where the heart of the column was, the heart of the enemy forces, to retrieve dead bodies of soldiers and to essentially truck them through half of the Zvornik municipality. And I would suggest that simply as a matter of military common sense, that policing up the battle casualties of your opponent in the middle of a battle as its occurring does not happen. So given when those particular graves are known forensically to have been installed and correlating with the military documents and everything else, I suspect that the military situation would not have settled down to a point where friendly forces, the VRS, for example, in this context, would have been able to begin sweeping the battle-field and policing up, should they choose to do so, policing up the remains of dead Muslim soldiers until well after the 23rd or 24th of July, 1995. So for all of those reasons, it is my opinion that the individuals that are in the four identified mass graves -- or the four identified mass grave sites in Zvornik are not battle casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I can only envy the State Department and the OTP for that kind of loyalty, but let us see whether you see think that this was static fighting or was the column on the move. Why would it be necessary to do anything while the column was on the move and they were leaving their dead behind?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just say I object to that kind of argumentive statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is: Do you claim that the Army of Republika Srpska, with a view to burying soldiers of the enemy army, would have to move through a maze of bullets in order to get the dead out, or was fighting taking place on the move? How long did a single column stay in a particular place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I would remind you that again with the size estimates of the column seeking to break through at between, you know, low numbers would be that Borovcanin used 2.500. There are much higher numbers, so between 3- and 7.000 people. My position is it's not one coherent battle, that it is a series of a large number of smaller battles that are occurring through various points of time as these individual parts of the couple are being encountered. So, you know, as -- as noted by Colonel Pandurevic's own reports, he does not have precise knowledge of where the enemy forces are at any given time. He's just giving assessments as to where he believes they're going. So in that particular environment to send, you know, burial recovery teams out into that type of military environment, quite frankly from a military point of view is ludicrous. No competent commander would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But is he talking about what was happening then or is he talking about what is to happen? Is he saying here that there aren't any forces for "asanacija"? That is to say that "asanacija" in the plural is what awaits him? Look at what he says.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His phrase is the additional burden is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout the schools, as well as obligations of security and restoration of terrain. I take that comment in a temporal sense as happening at that time. I do not read that as a future sense. I mean, given the context of an interim combat report reporting on the immediate and pressing issues, the fact that Colonel Pandurevic is going to be concerned at some future date about "asanacija" does not make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have any proof of the following: That Pandurevic knew about the execution after he returned to his brigade on the 15th, or is that yet another assumption?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, again I have not followed the testimony in this particular case, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think because we are going to move the previous part, we can continue, but, yes, Mr. Karadzic, move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you in general terms, Mr. Butler. In your report, what should be done for the following: In all those places where you say, "I believe," and "I assume," if we were to turn that into the affirmative, if we were to say "I know"? So could we do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would remind you that obviously I'm not a first-hand witness to what was occurring. As I note in many of the issues of various places in my report, there are a number of places where I draw conclusions based on inferences that I believe are not only reasonable inferences, I believe it's the only logical inference that can be drawn. Certainly in those particular instances, the Trial Chamber, I believe, is more than capable of reviewing those reports, and they have in the past, and making those determinations as to whether or not those opinions or those conclusions are beyond the scope of what the Trial Chamber requires out of an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you rule out all other possible explanations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. Much of my military analysis in this context was looking at various alternative situations. I mean, a perfect example was the issue relating to the Kravica warehouse massacre on 13 July 1995. You noted the fact that I had a certain belief. Frankly, I based that belief because of my ability to rule out the other possibilities. I mean, with Kravica, it's not particularly difficult to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, Your Honour, please. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session. Yes, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When one deconstructs that particular crime base and what happened at that time, once the shooting starts there are four things that are ultimately happen -- or could potential -- four potential outcomes for the individuals in the warehouse: As a result of the immediate shooting they're killed, it's an instant fatal injury; they're injured and their injuries are so severe that despite medical attention they will still die; the third option is that their injuries, with medical attention, will allow them to survive; and the fourth possible outcome is they will either not be injured or their injuries will be so slight that they will not require any medical attention. So you have four potential outcomes. And then if we use the figure of a thousand, just to keep the math simple for me, in one category of individuals who suffered almost instantaneous injury that was fatal, you have the number 997, and then all the way in the other category of individuals who were -- either suffered no injuries or such minor injuries that they were able to subsequently escape, you have the number three. Simply by random distribution alone you would expect to see individuals inside the warehouse who were subsequently wounded and then later died after receiving medical treatment or were wounded and survive after medical treatment. So as part of excluding the issue that this was a one-time impulse event as a reaction and that there was no ultimately premeditated plan to kill the individuals in the warehouse, investigatively we looked for evidence that wounded Muslims from the Kravica warehouse were brought to any medical facility. There are no record of them at the Bratunac facility, at the United Nations medical facility, at Milici, at Zvornik. There's no effort whatsoever to bring any wounded Muslims to be medically cared for. So even if I accept in argument the fact that the individuals at the Kravica warehouse, that the event was predicated by an impulse act of a potential escape, at some point shortly thereafter, somebody made a decision that the ultimate goal was that everyone inside that warehouse would ultimately be killed. So this is an example - I'm sorry if it's a bit long - of how we did look at, or certainly I did look at, from an investigative and military analytical sense all of the various alternatives before I came to a conclusion that not only the most likely alternative but the only logical one was related to a criminal act in that particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your report, did you present to the Chamber and other participants all these options and alternatives and processes through which you arrived at your conclusions? Did you explain this process of how your deduction and other cognizance exercises were carried out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. In the context of my written document, I did not. That was ultimately raised in various trials. Questions of my process and my methodologies and the assumptions that I used in various issues were raised both by the Prosecutors and by various legal counsel for the Defence in a number of cases so that the Court could completely understand the basis by what I was finding in my various -- the conclusions that I made in various reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, how can the Chamber arrive at a conclusion since you are providing speculations only? You claim that there was plan to kill all those people in the cooperative even though you know that there were only a few guards. You know that one of the prisoners approached the guard, tried to snatch a rifle from him, and it obviously shows that this was not planned beforehand. Nevertheless, you are presenting to the Chamber as a fact that that was planned, I don't know on the basis of which, and in addition to that you are working for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Setting the issue of bias aside, again I would remind you that the basis of my analysis, and again even setting the witness testimony aside, is based off the probabilities of various events occurring. The fact is I believe that there were more people there guarding the prisoners. It was not just a few people guarding nearly a thousand. Knowing the weapons that were used, because that evidence is available forensically from post-conflict evaluations of the Kravica warehouse. Again, when you lay all of those things out in context, even if I were to assume that the initial predicate event was a reaction to an attempt by Muslims to escape - and that were the only intent - you would see outcomes for other people in the warehouse that would reflect injuries that were treated at various medical centres. The fact is that did not occur. There's no evidence of that, and I know that investigatively that was looked at. So I'm telling you that I know things as a certain fact. I was not at the Kravica warehouse, but I believe that based on all of the information and looking at these groupings, the statistical groupings that were occurring, the only logical inference that can be drawn is that at some juncture a decision had been made that everyone inside that warehouse would be killed. Once that decision occurs, it is no longer an impulse reactive event. It becomes a premeditated plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, first of all, there was no attempt to escape. A rifle was snatched and fire was opened at the guards. Have you ever established the number of the guards that were guarding these thousand prisoners? Has everyone ever established the number of the guards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered this question. Why don't you move on. It's time for you conclude, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were 1.000 prisoners or a hundred or so prisoners? If there were 1.000 of them, where had they come from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an exact figure off the top of my head. Investigatively, I'm aware that the number of prisoners that are associated with the Kravica warehouse runs from a range of 500 up to a thousand. I just chose the number thousand to make the math a little simple for the example that I used. And my understanding investigatively, is that the prisoners who came from -- who were in the Kravica warehouse on 13 July 1995 were those prisoners who had been brought in either by vehicle or had walked from Sandici and Konjevic Polje. There may have even been prisoners brought in from as far as Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All of this in the area of "maybe," Mr. Butler; right? Did you see in photo images these thousands of prisoners in Kravica and on the meadows? Have you ever established the exact number of imprisoned people, or did you go along with the Muslim propaganda?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is all beyond his -- his evidence in chief he gave. He came as a military expert or military analyst to help the Chamber understand the military context.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Butler, do you think that -- but let's start with this: Once the column has passed through, under whose control was the territory of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before the column passed through, the territory of the Zvornik Brigade is under -- is under the control of the VRS, specifically the Zvornik Brigade and its commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you believe or do you have any proof that the hygiene and sanitation measures involving the burial of enemy soldiers was carried out in single graves wherever the bodies were found, or were they collected and then buried in common graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that as a result of the fact that many of the areas that the casualties from the column were located in had unmarked minefields and things of that nature with very few exceptions. It is my understanding that most of the people who fell as part of the column were not recovered until after the end of the war when mine -- mine identification units were going through those areas to mark off the areas for mines. That's why I believe that forensically there are distinctions made between those individuals who are fallen in the category of the surface remains, which would be most of the column, versus those individuals who are believed to have been victims of mass executions in various places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I am a bit concerned about what you believe. With the exception of Pobudje, which was in the area of the Bratunac Brigade, did you acquire any proof that there were surface remains found in the area of the Zvornik Brigade, and if you did, where were they found? As I said, with the exception of the Pobudje Brigade area of responsibility. No dead bodies were found, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
