utterances.text: Again, sir, I don't know the specifics of the surface remain retrieval. I -- that was not an area that I was required to delve into. It didn't have any bearing particularly on what I was doing, so I have no information one way or another other than my general understanding of when surface remains started to be recovered. I believe that there are aspects of the investigation related to Srebrenica which will reflect the more accurate numbers related to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on the route of the lorries, your conclusion is that they were transporting dead -- dead bodies. Now, as for other supplies such as those of ammunition, food, and other supplies, was that also carried out by lorries?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. I -- I don't understand your question. In which context are you referring to where you talk about -- I'm not making -- I don't assert that lorries were trans -- or moving the dead bodies with the exception of those vehicles that have been specifically identified as moving people from schools to grave sites. There were vehicles that were also carrying ammunition and other supplies. We have a comprehensive list of all of the vehicles belonging to the Zvornik Brigade. So it's pretty easy to distinguish from those documents what vehicles were carrying what.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said today that you managed to reconstruct the routes of individual lorries on the basis of which you concluded that those lorries were used for the transportation of corpses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What I said today was that in one particular instance which occurred on the 16th and 17th of July, by looking at the vehicle record of one lorry, we were able to determine that prisoners were carried from a position that corresponded to the 7th Battalion headquarter to a remote location, and then that vehicle returned, that it did not bring the prisoners to the higher headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade like it was supposed to. There are other vehicle records which talk about issues related to the bringing of prisoners to other places relating to the mass executions, and I believe that many of those records have been corroborated by testimony of various vehicle drivers who do describe what they were carrying on various days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you noticed or could you discern whether these drivers were aware of where they were taking those prisoners? Maybe they were taking them to a point where they would be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a general practice, the vehicle drivers, because they were required personally to account for the vehicle miles and the fuel that was used in the vehicles, kept generally accurate records of where they were going and what they were doing in those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was: What were they told? What were they told about the destination of the prisoners, and did you hear that they were surprised that it had to do anything with executions, because they were told that they were taking those people to be exchanged. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that generally a number of individuals who were dealing with prisoners were initially told that they were taking people to various sites to be exchanged, and I agree with your assertion that many of those people were quite surprised to learn when they arrived at various locations that the prisoners were not being exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read a report by the Dutch institute NIOD relating to the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that it would have been useful if you had read it, because we are talking here about a competent institution that dealt with the same thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I feel like it's time to cut you off. You said you would need 15 minutes, and now you are turning this witness -- trying to turn this witness to a fact witness. Conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I finished -- I'll finish shortly. I'm only going to show the witness one more document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read a report by the UN Secretary-General on the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with that report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I agree with it or not, because the conclusions -- I mean, there are many conclusions the report draws. I draw on the report because I believe it is a useful factual summary of the events that occurred up until the beginning of July 1995. The one note that I make and the one reason why I do hold a reservation on the United Nations report is that that report was in fact published prior to the trial of General Krstic, and I am sure that the United Nations did not have access to much of the evidence that was later used by the Office of the Prosecutor in the case relating to Krstic and other accused in the subsequent years. So kind of like my own reports which go up to the year 2003, while it may very well be accurate, it's got -- it has to be recognised that there is a larger body of information now available and that that should be factored into the general conclusions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of a recently given statement by Mr. Akashi and Mr. Bildt that pertain to Srebrenica? And, of course, the statements given by Mr. Stoltenberg, which speak of the fact that the war could have ended earlier and in which he also describes the conduct of the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I may have at some point been aware generally of a statement, at least by Mr. Bildt, who I think gave one many years ago to the Tribunal. I have not followed the proceedings here, so I do not know what, if any, of those individuals might have said about anything related to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have 1D5556. And this is going to be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, while we are waiting, you are, of course, familiar with the term "reductio ab absurdum," [as interpreted] which means that it would have been better to have the whole process rather than only the result.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the term, but I take it it's leading somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It should read "deductio ab absurdum," absurd deductions. But let's leave that aside. Have you ever seen this document that was in possession of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without an English translation, I -- I couldn't tell you whether I've ever seen this document or not just by the appearance of it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was disclosed to us by the OTP only three days ago, so we didn't have time to translate it. Can we now have page 2, and I'm going to read it to you. It says Geneva, 19th July, and paragraph 3 says: "In his speech, Bildt ascribed more critical comments and responsibility (for the fall of Srebrenica) to the offensive actions carried out by the BH Army and the HVO while he underlined that the Bosnian Serbs genuinely were more in favour of the cessation of hostilities." Now, did you know anything about this? Have you ever heard about these views of Mr. Bildt?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've heard an awful lot of points of view from a lot of individuals at various political levels in the international community about Srebrenica. They're not relevant to my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I regret to say that you have been biassed, but nevertheless, Mr. Butler, I would like to thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is this document being tendered?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, certainly. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So I think we'll have no objection, but it should be marked, Your Honour, first. We need to take a look and see what it is exactly. I don't believe we have a translation yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, let me reconsider. The witness wasn't able to speak to it at all and said it wasn't relevant to his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees no basis to admit this document through Mr. Butler. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I want to -- do you have your narratives with you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually do not today, sir. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. If there's no objection, I'll provide you with a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can upload it so that we can follow easily as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have the e-court page because this is something that just -- that came up today. If I could have paragraph 8.8. It's page 81 of the narrative revised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Revised narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, which is P04914.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where I'm going with this is you discussed the vehicle log and report when you talked about prisoners and executions around the 16th of July, and I'd like to just go to the 8.8 of your report and make sure that we're talking about the same thing. It's e-court page 86. Thank you, Ms. Raveling. And you discuss this at page 4 of the transcript, for the record, where you said there was a vehicle log for one truck from the 7th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, and we're talking about soldiers from the Krajina Corps. Is this the section you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Within the context of the discussion on prisoners being known to be in the custody of the VRS on the 16th and 17th. This is the document I'm referring to from the 7th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 02600, please. Page 3 of the English -- page 4 of the English, page 3 in Serbian. And while we get that -- and I'd like to look at the entries for 16 and 17 of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To save time, I won't go to the page, but it's in this. It's the vehicle work log of a TAM 2001 number M5342, which you also refer to in your footnote to the section of the report. Is this the vehicle log that you were discussing in your testimony this morning as well as in that section of your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just explain a little bit more why you cited this vehicle log and what it shows. I just want to give you the chance to expand a little bit on the answer you gave to Mr. Karadzic this morning about the relevance of this vehicle log and the document I'll show you in a minute to, as you said, the issue of prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade zone in the 16th and 17th and what did or did not happen to them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. I mean, in the context of my military analysis, there was a relatively clear understanding of the prisoner issues related to the individuals who had brought -- been brought up to the Zvornik Brigade area from the Bratunac Brigade municipality. What was a lot less clear was despite the fact that there are notations that the Zvornik Brigade is taking prisoners from the column, that there is no accounting for those prisoners in most documents. So this is one of the documents that I use to make the point that particularly on certain days, low-level units, in this case, you know, companies that were reported to battalions, there was prisoners being taken on various days. Now, if the -- if the processes and procedures that were supposed to be in place were followed, you would logically see an accounting for these prisoners at the higher headquarters when these prisoners arrived and were accounted for. And this is one of the documents I used to illustrate the point that there were individuals from the Zvornik Brigade who were known to have been in custody of prisoners that were taken from the column, and again in this case the 7th Infantry Battalion is nowhere near any of the identified other holding areas from where the mass executions occurred, so the prisoners could only come from the column, and yet there is no -- there is accounting for them anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just here we can see, I think it's -- it's obvious, but the section you're talking to -- about, for the 16th of July the notation we have number of people transported 1 plus 10, and transported food, ammunition, prisoners, and other things, and then on the next day again, transfer of prisoners. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4977, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could I have P04589. This is a Drina Corps corps command report. 06-244, which you cite in footnote 485 of your report on this section. That's paragraph 8.10. So maybe we could bring up the report quickly, same page, and see paragraph 8.10.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number again, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At paragraphs 8.10, same page. I think it was page 86 of the English of the narrative. P04914, page 86. And if we could blow that up so the witness could see his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So in 8.10 you relate a Zvornik Brigade regular combat report to this incident, and now I'll bring that report up, please. That's P04589. And again while it's coming up the question will be just how this report fits into the vehicle log and the point you're making in this section of chapter 8 on prisoner issues.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context it's not necessarily that specific vehicle log. This is in relation to the battle-field killings that occurred that I believe investigative we call the execution at Nezuk. One of the survivor accounts of that execution was that he either by looking at the patch of the soldiers' -- of the uniform of the soldiers who executed him or by learning it from one of the soldiers, did recognise that the soldiers who had him in custody were from the 16th Krajina Brigade, a unit that clearly is not normally part of the Zvornik Brigade structure. So what this particular document does or talks about in that context is that it notes that the presence of a company of the 16th Krajina Brigade in the Zvornik Brigade zone performing various duties. So this particular document actually talks about the fact that 13 soldiers were eliminated, two were captured, members of the 16th Krajina Brigade and a platoon were involved in that, and this particular document serves to a large degree to corroborate parts of the story of the Nezuk survivor as to how he came into the custody of the VRS and what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just briefly, Mr. Butler, the log we looked at - I won't bring it up again, and I'm done with this document - talked about bringing of food, bringing of prisoners. You were asked on the 20th of April at T-27767 by Mr. Karadzic about whether the proper way under VRS regulations was to bring prisoners to a collection point, and on the same day at 27733, you were asked about an intercept talking -- which was put to you that Colonel Beara is requesting trucks and trailers to take prisoners to Batkovici. So my question is looking as you did at the bulk of the evidence seized, vehicle log, et cetera, orders, you've already explained what you didn't -- what you didn't see in relation to some of these topics, but did you see any military, environmental, or other reason, looking at all the evidence, for the prisoners who were brought to Zvornik and just halted there before they were killed could not have continued on to Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, the narrowest portion of the road from a military perspective to where the front lines would be would be in the Zvornik and Karakaj area. The fact that bus and trucks filled with prisoners were easily able to continue northward, and in fact did, through Petkovci and Rocevic and Branjevo, there's no military reason why they could not have continued all the way to Petkovci. I mean, the road was not threatened in any sense. So the fact that they did not go to Petkovci was by -- I'm sorry, they did not go to Batkovic was by design. It was not as a result of military necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Karadzic asked you questions about whether truck drivers were told that prisoners would be exchanged when they were bringing them sometimes to kind of remote mountain top areas like Bisina, for example. Did you find any evidence that prisoners were somehow taken and actually were exchanged during the 14th, 15th, 16th of July in Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean to the contrary. As -- as I've noted earlier, by the 14th and 15th, I think by the early morning of the 15th, certainly the police and the military forces are aware that a senior police official had been captured by the column, and I know that there was a number of discussions that went back and forth relating to whether or not this senior RS police official was still alive and whether or not it would be possible to exchange him. At that point in time, one would think that, you know, Colonel Pandurevic and the Zvornik Brigade still had, you know, several thousand prisoners alive that had there actually been an intent to exchange those prisoners for this police captain, that they would have easily had the ability to do so. So there's no evidence of those types of exchanges occurring in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, one point you made during your cross-examination just now was about the killings at the Kravica warehouse, that there was no evidence whatsoever that you found that any prisoners were provided with medical care and either died or survived after medical care. What I want to ask you is just to round that out, what about the other major execution sites, Orahovac, Branjevo, Petkovci, Pilica, Kozluk. In any of those cases did you find that any prisoners had survived and been provided medical care?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two instances that I'm aware of. One instance is well documented where four individuals who apparently survived the Branjevo Farm massacre were later recaptured by the VRS. They were interviewed, and there were actually stories that were made as a statement as to where they were captured and everything else to camouflage the fact that they were massacre survivors, and I believe those four individuals are still missing. I believe I documented that in my narrative under the -- I have an addendum to chapter 8 about prisoner issues. I am aware of a second issue where a prisoner survived an execution I believe in Kozluk, escaped to Serbia, and then was later brought back and is now again missing. I'm not aware of -- with the exception of one instance, a child survivor of Orahovac, who did make it to the Zvornik Brigade medical centre. That is the only instance I'm aware of where people from mass executions, who survived them initially, received any medical care.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Kozluk survivor, I'll lead for a minute, is that Resid Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me move on now quickly to some questions about the corridor that came up today. There were some questions from His Honour as well as some follow-up questions by Mr. Karadzic. We looked at P04956. We don't need to bring it up now, but that's an intercept from the 16 July in which the Drina Corps is calling down to the Zvornik Brigade saying they need permission from the main head of state, and they're talking about the opening of the corridor. Mr. Karadzic in his questions talked about getting information from Karisik and that he supported Mr. Pandurevic's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to look at P01412, please. That's the 56th session of the RS Assembly session -- 52nd session, excuse me, on 5th August 1995. And if we could go to 19 in English and 17 in Serbian. That's it. If we can now go to page 19. Second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is Mr. Karadzic speaking: "As you know we had success in Srebrenica and Zepa. There were no objections or remarks on that success. Of course, many stupid things were done afterwards because many Muslim soldiers were wandering around in the woods and we suffered casualties then. Still, we did not suffer any casualties during the action." And then if I can continue now to e-court English page 23, Serbian page 20. What I'd like you to look at is the bottom of the second paragraph. Mr. Karadzic continues: "The Turks from Gorazde could get there whenever they want. The same as 9.000 armed Turks in the woods and mountains could have taken Srebrenica again." We scroll down in the English. "They could have burned Milici, Vlasenica and Zvornik. People from that area can tell you about it because it could have happened if they were smart enough and if they had a command. It's a landing division with 9.000 men. It could have been a landing operation. Only our men and dear God could save us. About 50 to 60 of our men got killed there trying to block them but several thousands of soldiers eventually managed" - turn the page - "to pass. And now Srebrenica division has been formed, lined up in Tuzla in order to get back to Srebrenica. We were not able to surround and destroy that enemy because we were in a hurry to get to Zepa, and we assigned two generals to Zepa to waste 15 days in negotiations with jackasses and idiots who are wasting their time instead of letting Rajko Kusic finish all of it or maybe General Krstic who proved to be very good." So my question is the 50 or 60 men that Mr. Karadzic speaks about who got killed trying to block these men from Srebrenica who were the Srebrenica Division in Zepa, what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those would be casualties primarily from the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, but there were some police casualties that were incurred on the 14th, 15th, 16th, and 17th trying to block the column from successfully escaping the territory of the RS. I think most of the casualties occurred the evening hours of the 15th and the morning hours of 16th July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, second question: Does this provide you with any information either way about the knowledge of the leadership of whether the men in that -- or whether the -- I should say the people in that column who managed to pass were soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I believe that everybody knew that the people who were in the column were for the most part either armed or unarmed soldiers or -- or at least military-aged men. As I've discussed earlier, in the -- you know, when -- when you look at the context of what happened on the 15th of July, you know, Colonel Pandurevic is not interested in letting the column pass. He's interested in doing a military solution because he believes he has the means to and he understand that that's the intent of his superior commanders. He only makes the decision out of military interest to let the column pass on the afternoon of the 16th for a discrete period of 24 hours because he essentially has no choice. I mean, he has no ability militarily to stop it. His units are obtaining significant casualties. He doesn't believe that the Serbian blood being expended to that point is worth the gain, so he does so. And, of course, by doing that and essentially defying his instructions from his superior command, he now has a motive to downplay what the actual impact of that would be with the fact of how many soldiers had been let out or military-aged men had been let out, and also to misrepresent the characteristics of that column, and this is where he starts talking about civilians being part of the column. And again going back to the earlier point, the other people there who -- aren't saying that. They're all noting accurately that what we were engaged in in that context was combat against a column of, you know, military-aged men, a significant percentage, you know, maybe up to one-half, who were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then last question on this and I'll move on. But in this session we see on the 6th of August where then President Karadzic says there were no objections or remarks on the success in Srebrenica and Zepa, and then complains that this group of men were not surrounded and destroyed. By that time, has -- as far as you know, has word spread about the mass executions in the Zvornik Brigade AOR? So this is 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir, and this is why I believe that this particular document, especially for me, was -- was very important, and of course I was glad to get access to it naturally after I had written my reports, because this particular meeting comes two days after President Karadzic is seeking to essentially dismiss General Mladic from the command of the Main Staff. Now, in light of my knowledge of the earlier indictments for President Karadzic and that he was indicted under 7(3), it's inescapable that -- you know, here we have, less than three weeks after Srebrenica, an attempt by the president of the republic to fire General Mladic who many would view as responsible in part for Srebrenica as well, and obviously that would have an impact on 7(3) and, in getting back to the earlier question, to Rule 68 obligations. So a big part of what I tried to do as part of my research while I was here is to find whether or not there was any evidence whatsoever that one of the motivations for President Karadzic really trying to leave -- relieve General Mladic of command was as a result of the orders he gave which resulted in the deaths of thousands of people at Srebrenica, if there was a way to divorce that somehow. If this was President Karadzic's reaction that, you know, this is what he was trying to do. And you know, this as well as all of the evidence that I've come across to date, there's no information that suggests that. The reasons that he fired or sought to fire General Mladic had to do with a variety of other issues, and nowhere is he saying, you know, One the reasons why I wanted to terminate General Mladic's service as the commander of the Main Staff, as well as other officers involved in Srebrenica, was because I do not agree with the illegal activities that occurred there and this is my way of seeking to remove them from positions of authority. So I see this as a very significant document in trying to address what were or were not the motives of President Karadzic for trying to remove General Mladic from the command of the Main Staff on the 3rd and 4th of August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 02269, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, I'll tell you, Mr. Butler, this is the VRS Main Staff military prosecutor's office guidelines for determining criteria for criminal responsibility, and I just want to confirm you were discussing a document at pages 7 and 8 today, in the context of the discussion Mr. Karadzic was asking you about, whether there were command and control issues because of the nature of the VRS conscripts. Let me put it generally like that. My question is: Is this the document you were referring to when you said that commanders were provided with information as early as 1992 about ways to deal with these problems of revenge, crimes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to -- I may have miscited you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's page 7 of the English, sorry. Page 23 of the B/C/S. I'd like to go to there quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look at the second paragraph under heading 3, criminal offences against humanitarian and international law. There's a discussion of crimes against humanity and how they occur. Is that the part you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I could go to page 8 of the English, which should be page 25 of the Serbian. Now at the top. Look at the first two paragraphs. It's generally about the responsibility of officers, including for officers learning of crimes. Is that -- were you discussing this section as well? I just want to see if I'm correct in the part you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And this is again where I note the fact that it's not the actual number of the officers which is responsible for the discipline of the soldiers. It is the willingness and ability of those officers to use the various criminal and -- law and military disciplinary systems in order to implement proper discipline within the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Cover page and those two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's actually, Your Honour, the English is nine pages. I would -- I would prefer to tender the entire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the B/C/S version is 36 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe that's because of blank pages inserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not a very good scan but we're talking about nine pages of text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't object to tendering the entire document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4978, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. This would be a good time, Your Honour, for taking the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Excellencies, just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That means you have more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do have more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much more, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Probably about 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We better take a break now. We'll have a break for now and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Almost -- almost done, Mr. Butler. Just a few more topics I'll try to move through quickly. The first thing is I'm going to ask you to cast your mind back to around March, April 2009. You were asked on 19th of April why there was no report in this case, and you answered that you weren't asked to write one. I'd ask you to just think about that. In March at a Status Conference, 24th of March, we told the Court we were -- that we thought you were preparing a report and would prepare one, and on the 15th of May, 2009, when we filed your 94 bis notice, we noted on it that it had been impossible to complete one by the dead-line. So just try to think back. Do you remember whether we had discussions about doing an addendum and updating the various reports and whether you had time to do it or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of the question from Mr. Karadzic, he asked if I was ever doing a specific report on the Supreme Command, and to my knowledge I was not asked specifically to do that. I was asked and having asked in the past whether or not it's possible to do updated versions of a variety of other reports, and my answer back generally is that my current work schedule just does not give me the opportunity to take the time that I need to be able to do that. So I expect that, yes, at some time you possibly did ask me to update some of the other reports and narratives, and I probably told you I was just not able to do that, but again I don't believe we ever specifically discussed a Supreme Command specific report like the Main Staff report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now -- thank you. You've helped me with that. Now a completely different topic, and that's Directive 4. At 27652 to 653, in cross-examination Karadzic put it to you that he hadn't read Directive 4. He said: "Thank you, but I tell you that if I had read this directive - which I didn't, because I didn't sign it," and then he continued. And he also asked you: "You have no proof that I read this directive or commented upon it; correct?," on the same section. So I'm going to ask you some questions about that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And first could I have P00970 at page 240 in English and 207 in the Serbian original. That's the 50th Assembly session, 15 and 16 April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what I'm going to do, Mr. Butler, is show you a few documents and then I'll ask you a question putting them all together rather than each one.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So I will be asking you about these.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I only say this: These questions may be a result of my imprecision. I asked about the time when the directive was created and not whether I learned about it later on. Perhaps this can save us some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Karadzic will stipulate that he read Directive 4 and approved it, then I can skip this whole line, because that's what I'm seeking to establish, that he read it and that he approved it for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Karadzic would agree to it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I could only comment on how I did not sign many of the directives, but at the time of this directive's creation and implementation, I was not familiar with it and there is no proof I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In that case I'll continue because that's exactly the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right now here this is General Mladic speaking at the 50th Assembly session and we won't go into it, but that was a long contentious session we know. The one -- the part I want you to focus on, it's in the top paragraph. General Mladic says: "Some of these decision were only presented to you, Mr. President, and others you participated as a member of the Supreme Command. Some of the directives you signed, not all of them, though. Before we constituted and oriented ourselves, I used to sign them." So keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I now would like to look at P01415. That's the Assembly session from October 1995, page 84 in English, page 108 in the Serbian. And while it's coming up --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we had this in Serbian, what Mr. Nicholls just presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let -- let us show the accused the B/C/S version of Mladic's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I hope I have it correct. I had 207 in e-court. It was a little bit hard to find because of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us continue with this 1415 first then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have a hard copy I can give to Mr. Karadzic. So then 1415, e-court, page 48 in the e-court, page 108 in the Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that we have P970 in the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to move on to the next one if possible. 1415.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to save time while it's coming up I'll read out the portion we'll see that I want you to focus on. This is President Karadzic speaking. "I have examined, approved, and signed seven directives. No one submitted the 8th and 9th to me, not even to read it let alone to sign it, because General Gvero and the others wrote whom they should obey. I cannot be held responsible for the events from the 8th and 9th Directive. I will not stand for that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can we follow? I think I saw that passage in the previous page, but it moved. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I didn't see it I'm afraid, Your Honour. My notes say it's page 84 of the Serbian -- of the English. That's the correct page. It's in the paragraph which begins: "We must look at army publications," second paragraph on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you referred to the passage that it says, "I have examined, approved, and signed seven directives."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and then says, "... but not the 8th and 9th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read that, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now the third document is D02149, a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I could have the English page 13 and the Serbian page which is 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what this is, Mr. Butler, the Defence put into evidence General Manojlo Milovanovic's notes of meetings and conversations with President Karadzic during the war period. And I would like you to read his 10 November entry at the top there. You can see particularly point 2, General Milovanovic has written that Karadzic will soon receive Main Staff directive number 4 regulating the activities of the newly formed Drina Corps, et cetera. I will -- and I therefore ask him to review and approve it. And then he continues his notes: "In the following days the Supreme Commander had offered suggestions, verbally approved Directive number 4, and returned it for the Main Staff commander's signature in view of the fact that this directive provides for issues of a purely military organisation." Have you seen that Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to skip ahead to P04248. Just to remind us we saw this before but this is the timetable. Keeping in mind that Directive 4 was dated and issued the 19th of December, we've seen General Milovanovic's notes from -- sorry, 19th of November, 1992, we've seen Milovanovic's notes from earlier in November. This military -- this timetable for the military and political seminar four days after directive 4 was issued, opening speech by the president and then the briefing by General Zivanovic. This is the 23rd of November. I won't bring it up again. But at P02716, Mr. Karadzic's notebook, we saw from that day, the 23rd of November, he wrote "Colonel Zivanovic," and then, "Tasks: Vitinica, Sapna, Teocak, Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, Gorazde." Do you remember that? We looked at that entry.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I want to move to the next day, 24 November, and then I'll ask you to some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a Drina Corps demand document, 24 November 1992, very urgent decision for further operations. I'll wait for it to come up. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, it's Exhibit P2085.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe I've seen this document at some juncture during the past couple of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And we that this is pursuant to the directive of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, strictly confidential -- I'll skip, 19 November 1992 directive, Directive 4: [As read] "Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up, or force them to surrender and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde," the same four places we saw written in Mr. Karadzic's notebook from the day before. So my question is: Putting together all these documents I've shown you, General Milovanovic's notes, the Assembly sessions, and the fact that this conference was held the day before Zivanovic issued the Drina Corps Directive 4 implementation, from your military analysis, what does that show about the Supreme Commander's involvement in the issuance of Directive 4 and the subsequent order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in -- in the context of the documents that have just been reviewed, whether he signs Directive 4 or not, the Supreme Commander cannot be ignorant of what the goals of objectives of that directive are specific to the Drina Corps in light of the fact that he attends a Drina Corps conference where to a large degree the details as to how the Drina Corps and its subordinate brigades are going to implement that plan are discussed. So I mean I don't see -- like I said, I mean obviously there is no signature from President Karadzic on the document, but in light of what happens with respect to the fact that he's at this particular conference and he's being briefed by the relevant commanders as to their military goals and intentions in light of the plan that they've received, the Supreme Commander can't be ignorant of that. He has to know this. What point in time or what day he may have read Directive 4 I can't possibly say, but he had to know what the Drina Corps's roles and missions are in order to participate intelligently in the conference that occurs on 23 November of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to quickly move on to another small topic. It was put to you on 20th of April at T-27725 to 27726 that it was only on the 9th of July that the Serbian forces considered the possibility of entering Srebrenica and you agreed discussing the Krivaja 95 operation plan. What I want to show you is a couple documents from earlier in the year to put some context into what the VRS's intentions may have been regarding Srebrenica and the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So if I could have 65 ter 02071, please. And while it's coming up, I'll also say it was -- you were questioned about Muslim forces attacks in June and that the Krivaja 95 could have been reaction to those attacks. This document from the 15th of May, command of the Drina Corps, it's signed by then a -- the deputy, Krstic, which states: "Urgent order to stabilise defence around Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves and establish conditions for the liberation of the enclaves." Can you just tell us what this document adds to the picture, if anything.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though we discussed as a pin point in time the Krivaja 95 operation, I mean, going back to Krivaja 95, the genesis for the intent there was incorporated in Directive 7 and 7.1, which came out in March of 1995. After that, you had a series of orders in the intervening months from the VRS and other units dealing with how they were going to implement various portions. This particular one talks about military operations to potentially cut the lines of communication of the 28th Division between Srebrenica and Zepa. So there was always -- you know, since -- since March of 1995, there was always that intent to do that. I guess the question is again going back to at what point in time did an actual assault on the town of Srebrenica become feasible as a military operation, and that's where I believe my testimony is that while it's not implicit in Krivaja 95's operations plan, by the 9th they had achieved such military success that that became a viable military objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask Mr. Nicholls to ask the witness to read out the first paragraph, because it's part and parcel of the document and it is also important to providing an answer to Mr. Nicholls's question as to why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I don't want to read out the first paragraph. I mean, the whole document if it's admitted will be there. Just for time, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4979, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 02072, document from the next day, also Drina Corps, also signed by Deputy Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just tell us what this is just to fill out this little chapter.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again as noted in Directive 7, they wanted to implement these plans against the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves as early as possible. One of the problems that they had was they did not have the adequate amount of forces. At approximately this time, Muslim military forces in both the 1st and 2nd Corps are carrying out large-scale attacks against corresponding VRS army and police forces, and at this particular point, they're noting that, you know, it's [indiscernible] to disregard the previous order because they do not have adequate military forces available in order to conduct them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4980, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P00168, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about a different topic now, Mr. Butler. This is from T-27734 to 35, a long discussion between you and Mr. Karadzic about the numbers of prisoners on the 13th of July and the aerial photo from Nova Kasaba, and I won't go through all that again, but it was put to you that commanders brag about the number of prisoners they've taken and that there were far fewer. This document, the same time as the aerial, 1400, dated 13 July 1995, from commander of the 65th Protection Unit, Milomir Savcic, and it states at the beginning: "There are over a thousand members of the 28th Division of the so-called BiH Army captured in the area of Dusanovo (Kasaba). Prisoners are under the control of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. Assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the Main Staff VRS proposes the following." Now when it says "assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs proposes," who is that, even though it doesn't say his name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be General Tolimir, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And my question is again based on your military analysis and experience and looking at all these documents that you have regarding the Srebrenica operation, when General Tolimir is making a proposal for what to do and how to treat a group of prisoners, is it feasible that he's got inaccurate, inflated information from the documents you've seen in the other evidence through bragging of lower commanders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, given the context of who this is being sent to as a proposal, I mean, it's being sent to the commander of the Main Staff, you know, one would think that General Tolimir would seek to be operating off the most accurate information that he was able to obtain before making such a proposal to his superior, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just very quickly as a follow-up, you talked quite a lot over the last few days about the logistics involved with so many prisoners, whether it's for ultimately a murder operation or the logistics that would be involved for transporting them, providing food, water, medical care, et cetera, just how important is it to have an accurate prisoner count when a force is taking thousands of prisoners for the logistical purposes you've talked about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's critical, because the number of prisoners that in your -- that fall into your custody have a direct impact on so many different military issues that have to be accomplished. The number of prisoners has an impact on how many people have to be detailed to guard these individuals, how many vehicles have to be detailed to move these individuals to whatever designated location, how much water needs to be ordered, how much food needs to be ordered, what -- what or how much medical support might be required. All of these types of what we would call life-support measures require some form of an accurate accounting of how many prisoners, even your best estimates of how many prisoners that are going to be falling into your custody or are falling into your custody so your rear-service professionals can deal with these conditions appropriately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 01952.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is my last topic. It's very quick, Mr. Butler. Again on the 20th of April at 27748 to 27749, there was a discussion essentially about reporting to the president. And Mr. Karadzic asked you about some reporting on the 15th of July and said: [As read] "Is this supposed to alarm the president of the republic who has a thousand other things to do?" And is part of your answer you said: [As read] "The second issue I would again note that the military was not your only mechanism to receive information, particularly information that would potentially alarm you." And then you discussed a report of prisoners escaping from Pilica. First question --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that's up here has no correspondence to that. 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This time I think I read it out correctly. It should be 019 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was waiting for the French translation to be completed. Now you can continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first question I was going to ask is in that part of your testimony you referred to a 15 July report of prisoners escaping from Pilica. Is this the document, the MUP document, you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you look at the last paragraph of this particular document, you'll note it says that on the morning of 15 July, a group of about a hundred captured Muslims from Srebrenica managed to escape from Gornja Pilica, Zvornik municipality. My understanding is that ultimately that that report turned out to be inaccurate, but in the context of what we were discussing, my -- my opinion is that, you know, a report of a hundred prisoners of war essentially who escape well behind enemy lines in -- in the northern Zvornik municipality would be in a report that would be of sufficient gravity so that it would be rapidly escalated and there would at least be inquiries as to -- excuse me, whether or not the information is accurate and, if so, what was being done to resolve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I -- and as you say, this report goes directly to Tomo Kovac, the deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4981, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us just check this. Is this being sent to the president?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll -- we can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no further questions now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Excellencies, just a bit of time, a very little bit of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you put the question, let us know what kind of question you are going to ask the witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is a fact that one needs to spell out precisely whether civilians were mentioned at the meeting and whether I denied insight into the forth coming action in Directive 4, or am I claiming that I did not deal with the details that are contained in that directive. Also let us take a look at this telegram which is being sent on the 13th of July from -- at 1400 hours from Borike that is 120 kilometres away. Does the time correspond to the footage we saw? So when the Prosecution is testifying, then they can twist things any which way they want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow you to put the second question, only the second one, to the witness. Further cross-examination by Mr. Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Butler, is it correct that that previous document, the telegram of Commander Savcic is being sent from Borike, which is far away from Srebrenica and Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba, and also that it is being sent at 1400 hours exactly? If necessary, we're going to have the document called up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we have the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P168.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Butler, could you focus on this. Is it correct that the telegram is being sent from Borike at 1400 hours?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what it says, yes, sir. And if you look at that first paragraph it says IKM, 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, Borike, at 1400 hours. So that is a -- the situation as they understand it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where Borike is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have a general idea. It's related to the Zepa enclave, but I could not tell you in terms of distance how far away it is from -- I believe your earlier question would be how far away it is from Nova Kasaba or Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know that Borike is above Rogatica and that there is a farm there at Mount Sijemic [phoen] where Tolimir offered accommodation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That aerial image, does this also bear the same date and the same time, 1400 hours?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I believe, if I recall correctly, the image is dated 13 July 1995, and I believe the image is approximately -- the stamp on the image is approximately 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Also, does the content of this telegram correspond to what we see in the image?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, would I go back to the fact that from the image alone I have no way of knowing how many people might be in that square. I understand what number you've raised. I can't -- I can't agree or disagree with it because I don't believe that the image that I was able to look at would give me any indication of just how many people were there other than a wild guess. All I would say again is that Nova Kasaba falls under the jurisdiction of Major Malinic who is Lieutenant Savcic's subordinate. Major Malinic would have, obviously, a vested interest in accurately reporting to his superior, and that information is then being used in a proposal by General Tolimir to his superior General Mladic. So again, you know, for a variety of reasons, military officials have a vested interest in trying to pass forward the most accurate information possible because they know that the information that they're passing forward will be used by their superiors in various decisions that have to be made in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the way it should be. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, again taking you to a similar example we discussed as part of my testimony, subordinates who were in the field engaged in military operations were purporting the numbers of individuals that they were encountering in the column on the 12th and 13th, and so even despite getting what turned out to be accurate information - because those superiors did not believe or discounted the numbers because they couldn't conceive them to be feasible - they made decisions that were ultimately incorrect because they had not accepted the full accounting of the numbers from their subordinates. So the reality is that even though factual and accurate information is transmitted up the chain of command, there are situations where military commanders might elect to discount or ignore or misinterpret that information for a variety of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just in fairness, Mr. Karadzic said is it correct that the telegram is being tent from Borike at 1400 hours. Mr. Butler can't see the bottom of the document and the handwriting portion in answering that question in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And the English probably the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Next page, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I guess the document was drafted on the 14th -- at 1400 but ultimately not sent until 1510 hours, so an hour and a half difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Although in Serbian it says "handed over" or "had handed in." So I don't know whether that would be sent. At any rate, this is what Colonel Savcic has, information from 1400 hours. Thank you, Excellencies, I really wouldn't want to take advantage of your goodness any further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Butler that, concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber as well as the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague again to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, for the transcript, I would just like to say that the Defence is surprised by the extent to which the Prosecution has been turning their own employees into expert witnesses who are supposed to be comprehensive and impartial. So the way I see it, the Prosecution is testifying on its own behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. You had another opportunity to raise it, and this is not the proper time for you to reiterate it. We can continue, Mr. Nicholls? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll need to switch, Mr. President. That always takes about five minutes or so. Or no more than that, but we'll need to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber prefers to have a short break. We'll break -- rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 2.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue with the next witness, we will issue two oral rulings. First, the Chamber notes the urgent motion filed confidentially by the United Kingdom on the 20th of April, 2012, seeking an extension of time of 14 days to respond to the accused's motion to compel production of seven documents filed by him on the 24th of January, 2012. The Chamber also notes the accused's response to the urgent motion filed publicly on the 23rd of April, 2012, in which he opposes the extension of time and urges the Chamber to dispose of the original motion to compel production of seven documents. He also asks that the urgent motion for an extension of time be reclassified as public. Given that the UK's urgent motion reveals that the parties involved have been engaged in discussions right up until 19th of April, 2012, namely one day before the UK's dead-line to respond, and that both the accused and the UK indicate that further negotiations may still take place in the near future, the Chamber has decided to grant the UK's motion for the extension of time. The Chamber therefore invites the UK to file its response by no later than 7th of May, 2012. As for the accused's request for reclassify the urgent motion, the Chamber has decided not to grant this request due to the detailed submissions made by the UK therein regarding the ways in which the parties involved have been trying to resolve this issue and the sensitivity of the documents in question. The Chamber also does not consider it feasible to order the UK to file a public redacted version of the urgent motion as the extent of the required redaction would strip the motion of much of its content. Finally in this regard, the Chamber instructs the Registry to forward this ruling to the UK Embassy in The Hague. The Chamber will now issue an oral decision on the accused's 70th motion for finding of disclosure violation filed on 29th of March 2012. The motion alleges that Prosecution violated Rule 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence by the disclosures on 28th of March, 2012, of three potentially exculpatory documents. The Prosecution filed its response to the motion on the 12th of April, 2012. The Chamber finds that the three documents were disclosed by the Prosecutions as soon as practicable. The first document was intended for use with KDZ493 who was a witness for whom delayed disclosure of 30 days prior to his expected testimony had been granted. This document was disclosed within one week of the Chamber's decision which granted the Prosecution motion not to call KDZ493. With respect to the second and third documents, the Chamber notes the Prosecution's submission that it only recently obtained the documents and also only received the Rule 70 provider's consent for their disclosure on the 16th of March, 2012. The documents in question were disclosed within two weeks of that date. Given that these three documents were disclosed by the Prosecution as soon as practicable, the Chamber finds that the Prosecution did not violate its disclosure obligations under Rule 68 of the Rules and dismisses the motion in its entirety. That said, let us bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djeric. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could we simply begin by asking you to state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Branko Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, is it correct that you have testified before this Tribunal in two previous cases, in the case of Prosecutor v. Krajisnik in July of 2006 and in the case of Prosecutor v. Stanisic/Zupljanin in October and November of 2009?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: That is all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you have recently had the opportunity to review certain excerpts from those testimonies and that during the process of reviewing those materials you also added a few clarifications or additional information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I call up 65 ter 90330, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you'll see on the screen before you a document that bears a signature and the date of April 5th, 2012 -- it's two signatures, actually, yours and Mr. Hogan's. Can you confirm that this is the document which contained the excerpts from your previous testimonies and added the few additional clarifications?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you also confirm, Mr. Djeric, that this document accurately reflects those portions of your previous testimonies and that if you were asked about those same matters here in court you would provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I would provide the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender the document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4982, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with the Court's leave, I'll proceed to read a brief summary. Mr. Djeric was the prime minister of Republika Srpska from 1992. Although he resigned in October 1992, he remained acting as the prime minister until mid December 1992. Although the Republika Srpska had a collective Presidency in 1992, it was a party state, which was in practice run by Mr. Karadzic and the party. For example, when the government was formed, it was Mr. Karadzic and the party who selected the candidates whom the witness would propose to the Assembly for ministerial positions. The government was a technical attachment, not a body that could create policies. Mr. Karadzic considered himself to be the government, and he and the people around him set the policy for the state. The minister of justice, Momcilo Mandic, and the minister of interior, Mico Stanisic, largely bypassed the government and reported directly to Mr. Karadzic. Mandic and Stanisic ignored Mr. Djeric and Stanisic threatened to kill him. Stanisic and Mandic were also involved in crimes. The witness wanted to replace Mandic and Stanisic but was prevented by Mr. Karadzic. Finally, in October 1992, the witness resigned because he considered that the government was not functioning. The witness had concerns about crimes being committed by Serbs. He wanted something to be done about this, but Mr. Karadzic disagreed, taking the position that these matters could be dealt with later. Mr. Karadzic dealt with the overall issues related to detention camps through members of the government with whom he dealt directly. Crisis Staffs were party organs. Representatives of the municipalities often came to the Presidency building to see Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. Representatives of Sarajevo municipalities more often met with Mr. Krajisnik, and representatives from Banja Luka more often met with Mr. Karadzic. Biljana Plavsic sought out and approved of paramilitary formations, a view she expressed at the 22nd Assembly session in Zvornik in November 1992. The witness testified that her opinion on this was not unusual and, as a rule, the Presidency approved of it. That concludes the summary, Mr. President, and I have no additional questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are tendering two associated exhibits, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first one, 65 ter 5542, which was discussed in para 25 of his amalgamated statement, I don't think he said anything. I think he said he doesn't remember such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's precisely the point, Mr. President. He was shown those documents and said those are the nature of the documents that he did not that -- he's not disputing their existence or their authenticity, but those are the types of materials to which he did not have access and which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it's because he --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] And in that sense they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The contents of the documents has been described sufficiently in that para. I'm not sure that document forms an indispensable and separable part. If you'd like to tender it, probably you better deal with it with the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure what additional information we could elicit. I mean, the -- the situation would presumably be the same, that this is not a document which the witness remembered at the time he was shown in court, and I wouldn't expect him to have any further data about that at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll stand by our practice that this document will not be admitted as associated exhibit. So we'll admit 1527, which is an order from this witness. Very well. Mr. Djeric, as you noted that your evidence-in-chief was admitted in -- in the written form in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you'll be further examined by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Do you follow, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I understood it, this is an abbreviated version of my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You signed the so-called amalgamated statement, which is an excerpt from your previous testimony. That was admitted in lieu of your testimony in chief by the Prosecution to save some time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor Djeric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we haven't got much time left today, I simply wanted to go through a couple of general matters for the benefit of the Chamber. First of all, do you agree that save for the fact that we may have heard of each other, we hadn't known each other before the multi-party system was introduced; that is to say, before the changes made to our system?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: That is correct. We did not know each other.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, just a second. Mr. Djeric, would you be kind to come closer to the microphone so that the interpreters could hear you clearer. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that following that period we did not come -- become close personally, rather, we had fair business communication?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were on official terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct or do you recall that as part of the SDS there was a cadre commission which, among others, proposed you to be made part of the joint BiH government as part of the Serbian quota, and the posts in question were won by the SDS at the elections?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't remember that. I don't know how the commission worked. I only know that I arrived on your invitation, and I came to see you as the party president. I never met any president of the personnel commission. It was an internal party matter since I was not a member of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am waiting for the interpretation, and could you please do the same. Do you know Mr. Rajko Dukic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I did know Rajko Dukic, but it has nothing to do with this. I knew Dukic as a company manager of the bauxite company from Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you had known him long before the period in question; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, not long before, but somewhat before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I told you that he was the president of the personnel commission of the SDS, would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember that. I don't know what is there for me to accept or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Djeric, I'm trying to establish the following: How come that you, who were not a member of the SDS, were proposed to me as a member of the joint government, and I called you to a meeting to see you, whereupon I agreed with that proposal? Did you know that I could reject the proposals of the personnel commission but provided I had sound reasons to do so?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I wasn't familiar with the personnel policy of the party, and there's nothing I can say with that -- in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both Mr. Karadzic and Professor Djeric, you are speaking the same language that should be translated into the working language of the UN, i.e., French and English. I would ask you to put a pause between question and answer. Would you please bear that in mind in the future. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Professor Djeric, that you were nominated for the position of development minister because of your theoretical knowledge rather than due to your managerial competencies as you had not worked in any company for a long time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: That is correct. When I came to see you, you agreed with the proposal. In other words, you accepted me as a potential development minister provided that the prime minister designate Jure Pelivan agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your system could Jure Pelivan not agree provided he had firm reasons to do so?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
